blocks.text: My name is Heidi Brandt. I was forty-three, a title examiner in Wauwatosa, Wisconsin, and a divorced mother of two. The only lock I had never changed belonged to my grandfather’s cabin.

On Friday, July 3, 2026, Maisie, twelve, climbed from our SUV carrying marshmallows. Owen, nine, spotted his sleeping bag on the porch steps and stopped smiling. The lake shone through the pines, familiar as ever. Everything else was wrong.

My brother Kyle stood in the doorway with a beer. His wife, Tessa, had hung towels over the railing. Hot dogs sat beside Grandpa Walt’s porch swing. My mother, Darlene, came down before I opened the trunk.
“You knew they needed somewhere to live,” she said. “Don’t make a scene in front of the children.”
“I knew Kyle lost his job. I didn’t know he moved into my house.”
She pulled out her phone. “Then we’ll let the sheriff sort it out.”
I sounded calmer than I felt. Owen rubbed his sweatshirt sleeve, something he did when adults argued. I wanted to take them home. But my mother had counted on that retreat all my life.

While she talked to the dispatcher, Dad appeared from behind the garage carrying a screwdriver. He went straight to the crooked screen-door hinge, as though he’d been assigned a repair. When I asked how long everyone had been there, he focused on the screw.
My father, Ron, could answer a question without ever going near it.
Tessa emerged with a wooden spoon. She looked genuinely surprised to see us.
“Darlene said you were coming in August.”
“I offered you two weeks in August,” I said. “That was all.”
She looked at Kyle. He examined the label on his beer.

I took Maisie and Owen to the porch swing, facing the driveway. I’d never sat there. Grandpa built it in 1999, after the original cabin burned, for anyone who needed a rest. My mother said I hadn’t earned that right.

I was sixteen when the fire happened, on July 4, 1998. Grandpa’s old cabin had cedar shingles and a stone chimney. Kyle was fourteen. He and a neighbor boy fired bottle rockets off the dock while Mom said boys ought to enjoy the holiday.

I had lit a citronella candle in a glass jar on the west porch. Mosquitoes were terrible. After setting my library book beside it, I went inside to dry dishes while Grandpa washed. We were halfway through one of his off-key country songs when he smelled something burning.
The roof was on fire when I ran for the hose. Flames climbed the east side near the chimney, far from my upright candle. I remember passing that small flame as clearly as I remember the roof’s heat.
Firefighters couldn’t save the cabin. I sat in the wet grass while Dad stood beside Kyle near the dock. Kyle held something small and silver. I thought it was a lighter, but nobody would explain.

Two days later, our family gathered in a neighbor’s kitchen. Mom announced that my unattended candle had burned Grandpa’s cabin down. When I said the fire began on the opposite side, she told everyone I was confused. Dad stepped outside with the insurance adjuster. Kyle stared at his breakfast.
Grandpa put his jacket around my shoulders. “Don’t apologize for what you don’t know,” he whispered. But he didn’t contradict my mother either.
She sent me to Aunt Carol in Ohio for the rest of the summer. By the time school started, I had rehearsed her version of that night so often it sounded like my own memory.

When I turned eighteen in September 2000, Mom showed me a photocopy with a bank logo. She said insurance hadn’t covered the rebuilding costs, Dad had taken a second mortgage, and my college savings had been used to make up the difference. I cried at the kitchen table. Then I agreed to repay the family $175 every month.

The transfer became as ordinary as the phone bill. I took community college classes while working at a title company. I learned to trace deeds, liens, and mortgages back decades, searching for errors that could cost strangers their homes. Yet I never examined the supposed mortgage shaping my life. Some questions still felt forbidden.

I married, had Maisie and Owen, and divorced peacefully. My ex, Greg, still drove across town when Owen forgot his inhaler. Mom called whenever somebody needed a ride or a check. I kept paying because I wanted to feel welcome at Thanksgiving.

Grandpa died in October 2023. He had recorded a transfer-on-death designation naming me as the cabin’s beneficiary, years before his death. I completed the necessary recording afterward, put the taxes and utilities in my name, and brought the kids up the following summer.

That first summer, Maisie learned to skip stones, and Owen insisted the little bunk by the window belonged to him. I kept finding reasons to stand instead of sitting on the swing. I had the deed, the keys, and still couldn’t quite believe I was allowed to stay.
Mom called the inheritance a mistake. This April, after Kyle lost his paper-mill job and his rental, she demanded I sign the cabin over to him. I refused for the first time in years.

Now Kyle’s mail sat in a stack inside my kitchen window, addressed to him at my property. Dad was repairing the screen. Tessa’s children were swimming by the dock. My mother told the dispatcher that I was unstable and had a history of causing fires.
The dispatcher said a deputy would come when one was available. Mom ended the call, went inside, and returned with a sheet of paper and a pen.
She laid a quitclaim deed on Grandpa’s porch table. My name was listed as the person transferring ownership; Kyle’s was listed as the new owner.
“Sign,” she said, “and you can stop paying for what you did.”

I stared at the deed, then at the hand my mother had placed over the signature line. She had already filled in the date. I could spot an incorrect digit in the parcel number, but pointing it out would only help her prepare a better document.
“Where’s the mortgage paperwork?” I asked.
“Don’t start using your job to confuse everybody.”
I put the pen down. My mother’s expression told me she expected an argument, not a question she would have to answer.

I had started asking questions in May. Maisie’s seventh-grade history project was about Little Tamarack Lake, and she had found an online archive of its association newsletters. In the August 1998 issue, beneath a photograph of Grandpa’s blackened chimney, the fire chief identified an aerial firework as the cause. The point of origin was the east roof, near the chimney.
“Your candle was on the west porch,” Maisie said. “Right?”

I printed the page before I trusted myself to speak. For years, I’d remembered the candle and doubted everything around it. Now a report written weeks after the fire confirmed what my sixteen-year-old eyes had seen.
When I called Dad, he said, “Let it lie, Heidi. Your mother has enough problems.”
He hadn’t asked what I meant. That scared me more than an angry denial would have.

I checked the county records. I found no mortgage against Grandpa’s cabin in Dad’s name. That proved little: Dad could have borrowed against another property or taken an unsecured loan. Still, Mom’s old photocopy was no longer enough. I needed original paperwork, or someone who remembered it.

On Memorial Day weekend, I drove to the cabin alone and searched Grandpa’s old desk for any mention of the fire. I found his address book, with a card for Gene Halverson, the retired insurance adjuster. At the bottom Grandpa had written, For Heidi, if she asks.

Gene answered my call. He remembered my grandfather and said Walt had given him a sealed envelope of documents to keep. Gene had promised to deliver it to me at the lake, face-to-face, if I wanted it. We arranged to meet July 5.

Then I arrived two days early and discovered my relatives occupying the place. While Mom called the sheriff, I texted Gene to explain. He replied that he could come that evening. I hadn’t told him about the deed; he knew only that my family was there and I needed him.
Back at the porch table, Mom folded her arms. “Twenty-six years of payments forgiven. That’s generous, Heidi.”

It took effort not to reach for the pen. I had sent her money on the fifteenth of every month since September 2000, including the payment two weeks earlier. There had been 310 transfers, totaling $54,250. She was offering to release me from a debt she had never documented in exchange for property worth far more.
Through the screen door, Tessa called my name. She had something to tell me, quietly, before my mother came back inside.

Tessa stood by the kitchen counter, still holding the wooden spoon. She told me Mom had arrived in June with Grandpa’s spare key, announced Kyle’s family could stay indefinitely, and instructed them to forward their mail there. She had even accepted $600 from Kyle for June.
“I thought you were helping us,” Tessa said. “I should have asked you myself.”
She looked toward the porch. That was answer enough. Tessa showed me a message where Mom claimed I had approved the move. She forwarded it to my phone herself.

When we went outside, Kyle was counting six hundred-dollar bills into my mother’s hand. Another payment, he announced, for July. Apparently my brother could afford rent as long as it went to someone who didn’t own the property.
I recorded the amount and time in my phone. At work, I wrote down every inconsistency before trying to decide what it meant. I was going to need that habit now.
My mother caught me typing. “Keep your little notes. The deputy will see a woman putting children out on a holiday.”
Then she walked toward the dock, where Maisie and Owen were sitting with their cousins. By the time I reached them, her hand was on Maisie’s shoulder.
“Your mother burned down this cabin once,” she told the children. “And she still thinks she gets to do whatever she wants.”
Brody, Kyle’s ten-year-old, repeated the words fire starter at Owen. My son started crying. Maisie lifted her chin and said, “That’s not what the newsletter says, Grandma.”
“Enough,” I told my mother. “You will not use my children to punish me.”
Her voice dropped. “If Kyle leaves, you don’t have a mother anymore.”
